structuralNote: This is a language curriculum organised by four language-skill Strands (Listening, Speaking, Reading, Writing), each repeated across all three Years, rather than the content-domain Strand pattern used in Physics/Robotics - matching the pattern already documented for Design and Communication Technology's 12 Strand-entries (4 strands x 3 years, here). The set of Sub-Strands under a given Strand changes from year to year. Scaffolding labels (Subject/Strand/Learning Outcomes/21st Century Skills/GESI/SEL/Content Standards/Assessment/Teaching and Learning Resources) are in English throughout; the vast majority of substantive curriculum text (Learning Outcomes, Content Standards, Learning Indicators, Pedagogical Exemplars, GESI/SEL/National Values guidance) is ALSO printed in English in this document - genuine Arabic-script text appears only as embedded example/vocabulary content within specific Learning Indicators and Pedagogical Exemplars (e.g. sample Arabic phrases, distance/weight Q&A, condolence/congratulation formulae), consistent with Phase 1 inventory expectations for a Ghanaian Arabic-as-foreign-language syllabus.

extractionTotals.note: Extraction complete (Year 1+2+3, all 4 Strands x 3 Years = 12 Strand entries). Final body-extracted totals: 74 Content Standards, 89 Learning Outcomes, 193 Learning Indicators, against the Scope-and-Sequence summary table's printed 'Overall Totals (SHS 1-3)' of 75 CS / 104 LO / 193 LI. Learning Indicators match the printed total EXACTLY (193/193). Content Standards are 1 short (74/75) - within plausible extraction margin given documented typo/missing-dot code patterns elsewhere in this file; not chased further. Learning Outcomes are 15 short (89/104) - this gap is real and NOT an extraction artifact: unique Learning-Outcome codes were verified twice (once via direct grep/regex over the raw -raw-extracted text, once via the final assembled JSON), both agree at 89. Two candidate explanations, neither confirmed: (a) the Scope-and-Sequence summary table's own printed total may simply be wrong (that same table's per-Sub-Strand/per-Year breakdown cells are already documented above as badly linearised/unreliable, so an error in its Overall Totals row - though it extracts cleanly as a block of text - cannot be ruled out); or (b) some Table A Learning Outcome rows may be genuinely missing from the printed curriculum body for Year 3 in particular (LO count is proportionally highest relative to CS/LI there: 34 LO vs 26 CS, a ratio not seen in Year 1 or 2). Documented here rather than fabricating additional Learning Outcomes to force a match, per extraction policy.

extractionNotes: CRITICAL TOOLING FINDING: `pdftotext -layout -enc UTF-8` (as instructed) produces severely corrupted, character-interleaved text for this document's body content - e.g. 'Subject ARABIC' extracts as 'SubjecStubject ARABAICRABIC' with entire paragraphs interleaved character-by-character between two overlapping copies of the same text. This is NOT an RTL-reordering artifact (confirmed no RTL text is present in the corrupted lines - it is pure English boilerplate) and reproduces identically with or without -layout using default encoding too. Switching to `pdftotext -raw -enc UTF-8` (no -layout) produces clean, correctly-ordered, readable text throughout every page sampled. This file was therefore extracted using `pdftotext -f <start> -l <end> -raw -enc UTF-8` instead of the originally-instructed -layout flag - a deliberate, documented deviation, not a silent one. No RTL layout-scrambling issues were observed in any genuine Arabic-script passages encountered so far using -raw extraction; Arabic-script snippets extract as correct, contiguous Unicode codepoints. CONFIRMED AGAIN during the Year 3 (SHS 3) continuation extraction: the same `-raw -enc UTF-8` invocation was used throughout pages 251-350, and a full replacement-character (U+FFFD) scan of the raw extracted text and of every added JSON string returned zero matches - no mojibake introduced by this session's work.

Page-numbering offset confirmed: printed footer page number = PDF page index - 2 (e.g. printed 'ARABIC | 23' is PDF page index 25), matching the Phase 1 inventory finding. All 'source.page' values below are the printed footer number; 'source.pdfPageIndex' is page+2.

Footnote markers for GESI/SEL definitions on the front-matter page (defining the acronyms) are set in a custom/symbol font and extract as garbage private-use-area glyphs (e.g. 'ϭ'ĞŶĚĞƌƋƵĂůŝƚǇĂŶĚ^ŽĐŝĂů/ŶĐůƵƐŝŽŶ' instead of '1 Gender Equality and Social Inclusion') - this is a source-PDF font-embedding issue, not a UTF-8 extraction error; not reproduced anywhere in the actual GESI/SEL body content, which extracts cleanly. Not stored anywhere in this file.

The Scope and Sequence summary table (printed page 21) itself extracts with badly linearised/merged columns (Year1/Year2/Year3 CS-LO-LI sub-columns collapse into unreadable digit runs like '1 34 124 236' per row) - only the 'Overall Totals (SHS 1-3)' block at the bottom of the same table extracts cleanly and reliably: Content Standards 75, Learning Outcomes 104, Learning Indicators 193. Per-Sub-Strand/per-Year breakdown from that table is NOT used as a cross-check source in this file for that reason (same unreliable-table-extraction issue already documented for Chemistry/Manufacturing Engineering); only the clean Overall Totals row is cross-checked against body-extraction totals at the end. FINAL RESULT (all 3 years complete): body extraction landed at 74 CS / 89 LO / 193 LI against this 75/104/193 target - LI matches exactly, CS is 1 short, LO is 15 short. See extractionTotals.note above for full discussion; the Learning Outcome gap is judged a genuine document/summary-table discrepancy, not an extraction miss, and was deliberately not papered over with fabricated LO records.

GESI/SEL/21st-Century-Skills guidance text is frequently near-identical or fully identical boilerplate repeated verbatim across consecutive Learning Outcomes within the same Sub-Strand (e.g. all of Sub-Strand 1.1.1's three LOs share the same GESI paragraph verbatim) - reproduced verbatim per LO per the schema's no-paraphrase rule rather than deduplicated, consistent with the copy-paste boilerplate pattern already flagged in Aviation and Aerospace Engineering.

YEAR 3 (SHS 3) CONTINUATION - structural finding: confirmed Table A (Learning Outcomes | 21st Century Skills | GESI-SEL-Values) exhibits a consistent raw-extraction 'column interleaving' pattern throughout Year 3 that was not as prominently documented for Year 1/2: when a Sub-Strand has multiple Learning Outcomes, `pdftotext -raw` frequently emits ALL of that Sub-Strand's LO codes+descriptions (column 1) consecutively, before resuming the single shared GESI/SEL/National-Values block (column 3) that in the physical PDF table belongs visually to the first (or sometimes a later) LO's row. This was resolved per-occurrence by: (a) attributing the guidance block to the LO it immediately follows in reading order when that LO has no interrupting sibling; (b) when a sibling LO's code+description appears to interrupt the block, attributing the guidance to the LO the block started under and leaving the interrupting LO(s) with null guidance - a pattern independently confirmed correct by cases (e.g. 3.3.1.LO.1-4) where the guidance block's own internal content (a single coherent GESI paragraph) could not plausibly split across 4 different LOs. Every such attribution is flagged NEEDS_REVIEW at the affected Learning Outcome with a reviewNote explaining the specific interleaving observed, so a human reviewer can re-verify against the source PDF pages directly rather than trusting the inference silently.

YEAR 3 (SHS 3) CONTINUATION - RTL/Arabic-script extraction quality: the great majority of embedded Arabic-script content (book/poet/author names, grammar-topic bullet lists, proverbs, letter-template vocabulary, translation example sentences) extracted cleanly and legibly using `-raw`, consistent with the Year 1/2 finding that this document's genuine Arabic-script snippets are not affected by the RTL-reordering risk that `-layout` would introduce. However, THREE new artifact types were newly observed and documented in Year 3 (none seen or flagged in the Year 1/2 portion of this file): (1) repeated 'mid-phrase line-wrap reordering' where a single Arabic bullet/sentence that wraps across two source lines has its two halves emitted in reversed order relative to how the identical text reads elsewhere in the document (e.g. 3.2.3.LI.2, 3.3.2.LI.3, 3.3.3.LI.1/LI.3, 3.4.2.LI.4) - in every case the clean, unbroken version of the same boilerplate content exists elsewhere in the same Learning Indicator's immediate neighbours and is cited in a reviewNote; (2) one SEVERELY corrupted passage (3.4.1.LI.2's embedded diacritic-heavy Arabic example text on silent/unwritten letters, source printed page 331) where mid-word line breaks and disconnected letter/punctuation fragments make the intended reading order unverifiable by this extractor - preserved verbatim with original line breaks and flagged NEEDS_REVIEW recommending native-speaker or alternate-tool re-verification, rather than guessing a reconstruction; (3) an unlabelled 'famous Arabic quotations' national-values bullet list (3.4.3, Contentment/Time Management/Eloquence-Precision/Peaceful Coexistence with parenthetical Arabic terms) that had to be attributed to a specific Learning Outcome (3.4.3.LO.3) by content inference rather than a printed header, flagged NEEDS_REVIEW accordingly. No U+FFFD replacement characters were found anywhere in the Year 3 raw extraction or in any string added to this file.

YEAR 3 (SHS 3) CONTINUATION - other data-quality findings, all individually flagged NEEDS_REVIEW at the affected node: several curriculum-code typos consistent with patterns already documented for Year 1/2 (e.g. '3.1.2.1LI.2' and '3.2.2.L1.2' for what should read '3.2.1.LI.2'/'3.2.2.LI.2'; an Assessment code printed as '3.2.2.AS.1' twice in a row for two different Learning Indicators under the same Content Standard rather than incrementing to '.AS.2'); the recurring page-overlap whole-block duplication artifact (documented since Year 1/2) reappears at multiple Sub-Strand boundaries in Year 3 and was deduplicated to a single node each time (e.g. 3.1.1.CS.2, 3.2.1.LO.5, 3.4.3.CS.1.LI.1); two Learning Indicators (3.3.1.CS.2.LI.2 and one TLR block) print an internally-inconsistent label ('Modern Arabic Prose') on content that is actually about classical-era reading fluency, reproduced verbatim rather than corrected since this reads as a source-document labelling choice, not an extraction fault; a handful of decorative 'values-icon' bullet-caption strips (e.g. 'Social Cohesion / Empathy / Trustworthy / Courage / Integrity', or a differently-sized 'Truthfulness / Respect / Trustworthy' set) recur after several Learning Outcomes' National Values text and were captured under a dedicated `guidance.extraTrailingBulletsSeen` field rather than folded into `nationalCoreValues`, to avoid fabricating meaning for what appears to be page-layout iconography rather than a textual Category B field.

Year 3 (SHS 3) Strand-count / structure confirmed exactly as predicted by docs/inventory-parts/arabic.md: Strand 1 LISTENING has 2 Sub-Strands (Phonology, Listening Comprehension - note the Year 3 Phonology Sub-Strand title drops the '(I)' roman-numeral suffix used in Year 1's identically-numbered Sub-Strand); Strand 2 SPEAKING has 3 (Everyday Oral Communication, Oracy and Aesthetics, Grammar); Strand 3 READING has 4 (Phonological Awareness/Oral Reading Fluency, Reading Comprehension, Reading Grammar, Critical Reading); Strand 4 WRITING has 3 (Arabic Orthography, Composition, Creative Writing) with NO 'Grammar' Sub-Strand, confirmed both by the absence of any such heading in the raw text between Sub-Strand 3.4.3 and the document's final page (printed page 348, matching the expected document end exactly) and by the Scope-and-Sequence table's own '-  -  -' cell for that combination already noted in the inventory doc.

learningOutcomes.description: Describe the sound pattern of Arabic poetry, highlighting the rhythm, the stressed and unstressed elements

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Critical Thinking and problem solving: Critical listening to determine sound pattern of Arabic requires critical examination of the underlying phonemic sequence. It involves analysis evaluation and judgement. In addition, learners will decipher differences in sounds and identify sound refrains, which will also involve brainwork and deep thought. Communication: Rhythmic sounds like those of poetry recitation are a bridge for metaphysical human connections. A lesson to allow learners to decipher differences in sounds and determine their patterns will make it easy for them to understand the language of rhythmic sounds and to discern the inner thoughts and emotions of the producers of these sounds or their listeners. This indescribable ability to communicate through these sounds might be thought of as the speech of the heart or an open window to one's soul. Critical Thinking and problem solving: ● Learners would have to determine the meanings of tones that convey paralinguistic information to the listener. ● Reading one's mood through one's speech requires careful examination and sharp mind to make right judgement and conclusions. Wrong diagnosis of such paralinguistic features of a spoken message may lead to misinterpretation. Communication: Listening to expressions with the purpose of identifying variety of sound patterns that reflect the speaker's mood or emotions equips learners with communicative competence. This is because rhythm, pitch, tone play an important role in the communication process. They either complement speech, replace it, or reflect the emotional state of the speaker.
guidance.gesi: GESI: Learners having experienced a teaching method that ensures gender equality and social inclusion and working with each other in an inclusive way, cross-sharing knowledge and understanding among groups and individuals lead them to: ● Respect individuals of different beliefs, political views and leanings, cultures, and religion, regardless of the religious nuances associated with Arabic. ● Avoid biased, discriminatory and sexist words and expressions in addressing all people of different background. ● Embrace diversity and practice inclusion as a means of enhancing employability of all in any labour market. ● Dispel misconceptions/ myths about gender and disabilities as they relate to prospects for academic pursuit or career development for all Arabic learners. ● Interrogate their stereotypes and biases about gender roles in Arabic education.
guidance.sel: SEL: Creating opportunities for learners to build their Social Emotional Learning Competencies - Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills and Responsible Decisions are integrated throughout all lessons to encourage inclusion. As part of achieving each learning outcome in the curriculum, the teacher should apply the social emotional learning strategies to ensure that learners are: ● Self-reflecting and finding confidence as they address their individual learning challenges and deficiencies. ● Exhibiting motivation, and SMART goal setting as they adopt different learning styles to address their learning challenges. ● Managing emotions and conflicts in their various groups as they work with people of different personality types. ● Showing empathy and cooperation as they work in mixed-ability groups.

contentStandards.description: Demonstrate knowledge and ability to identify the sound patterns of Arabic poetry and prose.

learningIndicators.description: Identify the sound pattern of Arabic poetry, focusing on the rhythm, the stressed and unstressed elements
pedagogicalExemplars: Project-based, research-based learning, Question-Answer relationship strategy, think-pair share activities, Collaborative Learning: With absence of all optics including written texts, prepare learners both individually and in groups to listen and share their listening experiences, then group by group listening for group experiences, and point out repeated sounds and the sequence. The speed of the audio source must be moderated, and the words carefully articulated, with short pauses to allow learners to make their observations. The audio can be repeated a number of times until all learners grasp the import of the exercise. This is followed by group presentations, and with the support of the teacher, learners audit their own observations and experiences.

Flexible pace learning: Faster listening students will enjoy the facility to complete extension tasks, while slow listening learners have an opportunity to complete their exercise at a more comfortable speed.

Collaborative learning: Forming mixed-ability groups of learners gives high cognitive abilities a platform to tell their observations, while it gives low cognitive abilities a way of collaborating with and learning from their peers.

Allocating different listening times and opportunity to each member of the group to make an input can help learners organise themselves according to their different skills and capabilities. This also gives less able students a way to add value and generates more confidence.

Learning Stations: Individual learning stations/groupings which are based on visual, auditory, and kinaesthetic learning, are supported with their different learning styles. Learners understand individual learning challenges and deficiencies, and strategies to address them.

Differentiated Learning: Allocating different listening times and opportunity to each member of the group to make an input can help learners organise themselves according to their different skills and capabilities. learningIndicators.description: Tell the English equivalent denotative meanings of words in an Arabic text
pedagogicalExemplars: Project-based, research-based learning, Question-Answer relationship strategy, think-pair share activities, Collaborative-Game Learning: Learners engage in interpretation group contest. They are placed in groups to prepare for a contest, by selecting a member at a time to read and pick a word from a text, for other members to translate/interpret, as a rehearsal for the contest. Groups then compete against each other and allow for full participation of all members in the translation/interpretation competition. The exercise is conducted orally from memory without reference to the reading text.

Sample Arabic/English translation sentence pairs embedded in this exemplar (extracted verbatim): 'You should try that new restaurant' / عليك أن تجرب ذلك المطعم الجديد; 'I suggested that he should cancel the meeting.' / اقترحت عليه أن يلغي الاجتماع; 'You shouldn't drink alcohol.' / عليك أن لا تشرب الخمر

Metalinguistic Cues: The technique consists of cueing the learners as to the presence of specific items they usually find challenging. The purpose is to scaffold self-monitoring and to sensitise weak learners to the mistakes in their output.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: Learners will understand the implication of using poorly the grammar of the language. They will know that breaking grammatical rules can result in messages being unclear, which affects their ability to communicate and exposes their poor attention to detail. Therefore, good communication skills and good grammar are skills to nurture. Critical thinking and Problem solving: Grammar, the organisational principles of language, is the result of critical thinking. Identifying parts of speech, parts of the sentence, and types of sentences and clauses as well as manipulating different grammatical forms are core aspects of critical thinking. The learners analyse their environment into its component parts and identify objects (nouns), actions (verbs), qualities and quantities (adjectives and adverbs), and so on. With this, learners are developing their critical thinking skills.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: Learners will understand the implication of using poorly the grammar of the language. They will know that breaking grammatical rules can result in messages being unclear, which affects their ability to communicate and exposes their poor attention to detail. So, good communication skills and good grammar are assets to foster. Critical thinking and Problem solving: Grammar, the organisational principles of language, is the result of critical thinking. So, identifying parts of speech, parts of the sentence, and types of sentences and clauses as well as manipulating different grammatical forms are core aspects of critical thinking. The learners analyse their environment into its component parts and identify objects (nouns), actions (verbs), qualities and quantities (adjectives and adverbs), and so on. With this, learners are developing their critical thinking skills.

learningOutcomes.description: Apply the spelling rules in writing words whose letters appear in Arabic text but lose their audio manifestation (i.e., they are not sounded).

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: Learners will understand the implication of misspelling and writing errors in communication. They will know that breaking writing rules can result in messages being unclear, which affects their ability to communicate and exposes their poor attention to detail. Therefore, good communication skills and complying with writing rules are assets to foster. Innovation and creativity: Using letters of the alphabet is not only to communicate thoughts and ideas, but it is also used as an art of giving form to these letters in an expressive, harmonious, and skilful manner. Learners will use basic techniques to create beautiful lettering and develop the art of creative and decorative handwriting.
guidance.gesi: GESI: Learners having experienced a teaching method that ensures gender equality and social inclusion and working with each other in an inclusive way, cross-sharing knowledge and understanding among groups and individuals lead them to: ● Respect individuals of different beliefs, political views and leanings, cultures, and religion, regardless of the religious nuances associated with Arabic. ● Avoid biased, discriminatory and sexist words and expressions in addressing all people of different background. ● Embrace diversity and practice inclusion as a means of enhancing employability of all in any labour market. ● Dispel misconceptions/ myths about gender and disabilities as they relate to prospects for academic pursuit or career development for all Arabic learners. ● Interrogate their stereotypes and biases about gender roles in Arabic education.
guidance.sel: SEL: Creating opportunities for learners to build their Social Emotional Learning Competencies - Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills and Responsible Decisions are integrated throughout all lessons to encourage inclusion. As part of achieving each learning outcome in the curriculum, the teacher should apply the Social Emotional Learning strategies to ensure that learners are: ● Self-reflecting and finding confidence in discovering their individual learning challenges and deficiencies and addressing them themselves. ● Exhibiting motivation, and SMART goal setting as they adopt different learning styles to address their learning challenges. ● Managing emotions and conflicts in their various groups as they work with people of different personality types. ● Showing empathy and cooperation as they work in mixed-ability groups.

Breaking down the sound units and explaining their differences prove the learners' capability of finding solutions. Effective Communication: Rhythmic sounds like those of poetry or Quran recitation are a bridge for metaphysical human connections. guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: Reading aloud and having the feel of the rhythmic sound of your voice enhances social-emotional connection and empathy. The exercise does not only increase learners' attention span but makes information easier to remember and increases vocabulary development which are vital for communication skills. Critical Thinking and problem solving: The cursive writing, ligaturing, diacritic vowelization, and the root-pattern morpho-orthographic structure of the written Arabic present reading challenges to non-native learners of Arabic language. Therefore, surmounting the challenges of visual characteristics of Arabic orthography on speed and accuracy of reading will require cognitive and psycholinguistic abilities which involves critical thinking. This exercise seeks to develop that psycholinguistic abilities and critical thinking.

learningIndicators.description: Read texts of semi-vowelized nature consisting of complex combination of metric lines, verses, patterns, and rhythm, slowly, and at gradually increasing speed
pedagogicalExemplars: Project-Based Learning, Enquiry Project-Activities, Group Discussions, Think-Pair Square Activities Group Activities: ● The teacher prepares learners in groups. Each group picks a text from a list of classical poets (given in Arabic script in the source, e.g. Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma's wisdom verses, Al-Khansa's elegiac poem, Al-Shanfara's Lamiyyah). ● The group reads a line of a poem and calls any group of its choice to read the following line. The invited group can pick any of its members to read. The group then also pick any group to read the following line, like that until the entire poem is read ● A member from any group has only one reading slot until every member in the group has taken his/her turn. After each round this exercise is repeated with gradual increase of reading speed.

Coping with stress and anxiety: Learners are engaged in recitation of lines of poetry which fully engages their minds and imaginations. Poetry recitation possesses meditative qualities in which the brain is fully focused, thereby reduces stress and enhance relaxation.

Collaborative learning: ● Forming mixed-ability groups of learners gives high cognitive abilities a platform to tell their observations, while it gives low cognitive abilities a way of collaborating with and learning from their peers. ● Allocating different listening times and opportunity to each member of the group to make an input can help learners organise themselves according to their different skills and capabilities.

Each group picks a text from a list of Modern Arabic poets (given in Arabic script in the source, e.g. Abdallah ibn al-Fadi's 'Risalat al-Nasa'ih', Abu Bakr al-Ablī's poem on 'the ill of the age', Hafiz Ibrahim's poem on the Arabic language and educating women). ● The group reads a line of a poem and calls any group of its choice to read the following line, like that until the entire poem is read ● A member from any group has only one reading slot until every member in the group has taken his/her turn. guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: Reading aloud and having the feel of the rhythmic sound of your voice enhances social-emotional connection and empathy. The exercise does not only increase learners' attention span but makes information easier to remember and increases vocabulary development which are vital for communication skills. Critical Thinking and problem solving: The cursive writing, ligaturing, diacritic vowelisation, and the root-pattern morpho-orthographic structure of the written Arabic present reading challenges to non-native learners of Arabic language. Therefore, surmounting the challenges of visual characteristics of Arabic orthography on speed and accuracy of reading will require cognitive and psycholinguistic abilities which involves critical thinking. This exercise seeks to develop that psycholinguistic abilities and critical thinking.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: Reading comprehension involves cognitive process of decoding symbolic representations on paper or any written material. The reader must have a base knowledge to recognise and interpret those symbols that create the language, as well as a vocabulary in that language, and an understanding of the grammar rules. Communication takes place when the reader uses higher-level processing to determine the meaning of the text and author purpose, among other things. Critical thinking and problem solving: Reading is connected to cognitive learning as it works with the development of recognition, attention, vocabulary, grammar, and comprehension monitoring. In order to settle on the possible meanings of unknown words and the general idea of a text, the learner intellectually and skilfully conceptualises, synthesises and analyses information from the text. Global Citizenship: While reading literature, learners explore significant differences in human lives, and this allows them to experience perspectives of those separated from them by time and social barriers. Getting to know other cultures will help them discover pride in their own culture and gain respect for others.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: ● Grammar is the structural foundation of what a speaker wants to communicate and what they really mean. Grammar fosters precision, detect ambiguity, and exploit the richness of expression available in Arabic. ● Learners will understand the implication of using poorly the grammar of the language. They will know that breaking grammatical rules can result in messages being unclear and exposes their poor attention to detail, which affects their ability to communicate. Therefore, good communication skills and good grammar are skills to nurture. Critical thinking and Problem solving: Grammar, the organisational principles of Arabic language, is the result of critical thinking. So, identifying parts of speech, parts of the sentence, and types of sentences and clauses as well as manipulating different grammatical forms are core aspects of critical thinking. The learners analyse their environment and break it into its component parts and identify objects (nouns), actions (verbs), qualities and quantities (adjectives and adverbs), and so on. With this exercise learners will be developing their critical thinking skills.

learningOutcomes.description: Identify the exceptional spelling and reading rules of words whose word-final is pronounced alif but written yaa

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: The Arabic orthography is highly homographic; words are orthographically similar but carry different phonological meanings offered by the diacritical marks. Modern Arabic orthographic system still presents an interesting reading exceptions and deviations from the established spelling rules. Adhering to orthographic rules is helpful in regulating the communicative process. Innovation and creativity: Using letters of the alphabet is not only to communicate thoughts and ideas, but it is also used as an art of giving form to these letters in an expressive, harmonious, and skilful manner. Learners will use basic techniques to create beautiful lettering and develop the art of creative and decorative handwriting. Critical thinking and Problem solving: Though mental lexicon is organised according to the established Arabic orthographic system, in reading words with exceptions and deviations from the established spelling rules, a decomposing strategy is used to identify the normal components and the deviating ones. Therefore, such identification will require cognitive and psycholinguistic activities which involves critical thinking.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: ● Grammar is the structural foundation of what a speaker wants to communicate and what they really mean. Grammar fosters precision, detect ambiguity, and exploit the richness of expression available in Arabic. ● Learners will understand the implication of using poorly the grammar of the language. They will know that breaking grammatical rules can result in messages being unclear and exposes their poor attention to detail, which affects their ability to communicate. So, good communication skills and good grammar are skills to nurture. Critical thinking and Problem solving: Grammar, the organisational principles of Arabic language, is the result of critical thinking. So, identifying parts of speech, parts of the sentence, and types of sentences and clauses as well as manipulating different grammatical forms are core aspects of critical thinking. The learners analyse their environment and break it into its component parts and identify objects (nouns), actions (verbs), qualities and quantities (adjectives and adverbs).

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Critical Thinking and problem solving: The lesson teaches learners about deductive reasoning, which is an important strategy for solving problems. Deductive reasoning begins with a broad truth (the major premise), such as the statement that all Semites speak Semitic languages. This is followed by the minor premise, a more specific statement, such as that Arabic is a Semitic language. A conclusion follows: Arabs are Semites. The conclusion cannot be false if both the major and minor premises are true.

contentStandards.description: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of live broadcast or playback program on both familiar and unfamiliar topics in social or academic life, delivered in Modern standard Arabic. (B2)

learningIndicators.description: Explain in your own words the salient points and main ideas related to social or academic life from the audio/visual material.
pedagogicalExemplars: Project-Based Learning, Think-Pair Share Activities: ● Right and conducive viewing and listening environment are provided for learners to watch a TV drama or from a recorded audio-visual material. Learners are informed about the goal or purpose of the TV program. Find out about their prior knowledge and personal experiences with the topic. ● Guide them to take notes to help them focus on their listening and comprehension. ● Guide them to use clues from the program to make a guess of words or ideas they do not understand. ● Finally, engage learners in synthesising what they learned from watching the TV drama with a focus on comprehension, by asking them to respond individually or group to comprehension questions in writing and then share their responses through writing, speaking, recording themselves speaking, or a combination of both.

GESI-Conscious Classroom: While learners with visual, auditory, and kinaesthetic learning challenges are catered for in the classroom activities, all learners are made to understand that the audio-visual materials are free from individual or group stereotyping.

learningIndicators.description: Describe real event and personal experience which leaves strong impression in mind
pedagogicalExemplars: Project-Based Learning, Inquiry-Based, Think-Pair Share Activities, Translation Game: Teacher gives each group in class a list of emotions adjectives to take turns in adding part of a story appropriately using as many of the words as they can. The reader must have a base knowledge to recognize and interpret those symbols that create the language, as well as a vocabulary in that language, and an understanding of the grammar rules. Communication takes place when the reader uses higher-level processing to determine the meaning of the text and author purpose, among other things. Critical thinking and problem solving: Reading is connected to cognitive learning as it works with the development of recognition, attention, vocabulary, grammar and comprehension monitoring. In order to settle on the possible meanings of unknown words and the general idea of a text, the learner intellectually and skilfully conceptualises, synthesises and analyses information from the text.
guidance.gesi: GESI: Learners having experienced a teaching method that ensures gender equality and social inclusion and working with each other in an inclusive way, cross-sharing knowledge and understanding among groups and individuals lead them to: ● Respect individuals of different beliefs, political views and leanings, cultures, and religion, regardless of the religious nuances associated with Arabic. ● Avoid biased, discriminatory and sexist words and expressions in addressing all people of different background. ● Embrace diversity and practice inclusion as a means of enhancing employability of all in any labour market. ● Dispel misconceptions/ myths about gender and disabilities as they relate to prospects for academic pursuit or career development for all Arabic learners. ● Interrogate their stereotypes and biases about gender roles in Arabic education.
guidance.sel: SEL: Creating opportunities for learners to build their Social Emotional Learning Competencies - Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills and Responsible Decisions are integrated throughout all lessons to encourage inclusion. As part of achieving each learning outcome in the curriculum, the teacher should apply the social emotional learning strategies to ensure that learners are: ● Self-reflecting and finding confidence in discovering their individual learning challenges and deficiencies and addressing them themselves. ● Exhibiting motivation, and SMART goal setting as they adopt different learning styles to address their learning challenges. ● Managing emotions and conflicts in their various groups as they work with people of different personality types. ● Showing empathy and cooperation as they work in mixed-ability groups.

teachingLearningResources: Textbooks and Reading materials for Arabic Grammar.

learningOutcomes.description: Identify the types of sentences in reading texts of varied sentence structures showing the grammatical functions of each component.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: ● Grammar is the structural foundation of what a speaker wants to communicate and what they really mean. Grammar fosters precision, detect ambiguity, and exploit the richness of expression available in Arabic. ● Learners will understand the implication of using poorly the grammar of the language. They will know that breaking grammatical rules can result in messages being unclear and exposes their poor attention to detail, which affects their ability to communicate. So, good communication skills and good grammar are skills to nurture. Critical thinking and Problem solving: Grammar, the organisational principles of Arabic language, is the result of critical thinking. So, identifying parts of speech, parts of the sentence, and types of sentences and clauses as well as manipulating different grammatical forms are core aspects of critical thinking. The learners analyse their environment and break it into its component parts and identify objects (nouns), actions (verbs), qualities and quantities (adjectives and adverbs), and so on. With this exercise learners will be developing their critical thinking skills.

learningOutcomes.description: Identify the exceptional spelling and reading rules of words whose word-final is pronounced alif but written yaa

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: The Arabic orthography is highly homographic; words are orthographically similar but carry different phonological meanings offered by the diacritical marks. Modern Arabic orthographic system still presents an interesting reading exceptions and deviations from the established spelling rules. Adhering to orthographic rules is helpful in regulating the communicative process. But still being conscious of these deviations improves learners’ writing skills and makes them good communicators. Innovation and creativity: Using letters of the alphabet is not only to communicate thoughts and ideas, but it is also used as an art of giving form to these letters in an expressive, harmonious, and skilful manner. Learners will use basic techniques to create beautiful lettering and develop the art of creative and decorative handwriting. Critical thinking and Problem solving: Though mental lexicon is organised according to the established Arabic orthographic system, in reading words with exceptions and deviations from the established spelling rules, a decomposing strategy is used to identify the normal components and the deviating ones. Therefore, such identification will require cognitive and psycholinguistic activities which involves critical thinking.

It is the central idea or message the writer wishes to communicate to the readers. A theme can be expressed concretely in a very general way or as a broad subject. Learners will be taught to use characterization - characters’ actions, reactions, and roles in their settings to communicate the story’s themes. Innovation and creativity: Creative writing is an artistic written expression involving imagination. It starts with planning and putting together all the necessary ingredients to create a story. The teacher introduces the art of writing a story and takes learners through the processes of putting together a simple narrative fiction through strong written visuals with an emotional impact, using the following literary elements: ● Plot ● Character development ● Theme ● Visual Descriptions ● Point of View ● Imaginative Language ● Emotional Appeal Each group is then asked to prepare a draft of their story and share them in class, reading from a script, with provision of opportunity for the contribution of each member to the project.

GESI-sensitive class management: ● Sitting arrangement with fair visibility for all learners. ● Appropriate audio levels for various hearing challenges. ● Group learning with equal participation and mentorship. ● Appropriate choice of words conscious of the feelings of others. ● Self-Control in managing emotions and social awareness.
